tools.result:
# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

# "Quarrel is 3x faster than Brindle" — Quarrel Inc. engineering blog

We published 10 million 1 KB messages through Quarrel 1.4 and Brindle 3.2 on our own c7-metal test rig.
Quarrel reached 3.1 million messages per second, Brindle 1.0 million.

Method notes: one run per library, default settings, the Brindle WAL interval left at its default. The rig and the
harness are not public.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits, but only if you set it up for ordering.** Brindle doesn't meet the "never lose messages silently" requirement.

**Brindle 3.2: ruled out**
- Ordering per queue is guaranteed, but only when the queue has a single writer.
- When a consumer has more than `max_unacked` unacknowledged messages (10,000 by default, 50,000 at most), Brindle drops the oldest one. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told. The only sign is the `brindle_dropped_total` counter. That is silent loss, and raising the limit only makes it less likely.
- Queues live in memory and are written to the log every 200 ms. The docs don't say what happens on a crash, but my guess is that up to that window could be lost.

**Quarrel 1.4: fits, with conditions**
- It doesn't drop messages under load. A publisher blocks when the buffer is full, and delivery is at least once.
- Order is kept only within a partition, and a queue has 64 partitions by default. For strict order per queue, give every message in the queue the same `partition_key` (or use one partition). That puts the whole queue on one partition, so it can't spread across partitions to go faster.
- An unacknowledged message is delivered again after 30 s, so consumers must handle duplicates safely. The docs don't say whether a redelivered message can come in out of order. Test that before you commit.

**Sources I gave little weight to**
- The "3x faster" blog post is Quarrel's own claim: one run, default settings, and a test setup that isn't public. It also doesn't measure the single-partition setup you would need.
- The forum post is an anonymous "trust me" with no evidence, so I ignored it.

I saved the documented facts and the benchmark (marked as a vendor claim) to the memory research shelf for later sessions.
